repos.title: AIPOCH Open-Science: An Open-Source AI Research Workbench with Reproducible .science Packages
repos.paper_summary: AIPOCH Open-Science is an open-source AI research workbench that exports and imports research sessions as portable `.science` packages. The package keeps recorded relations among task context, executed activities, artifact versions, reviews and retained files, and it maps identifiers to the receiving workspace. The authors specify this exchange contract and test it on one controlled session with an incorrect first output, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision and a planned but unexecuted permutation test. Complete and partial exports were compared with source snapshots extracted independently of the exporter, and both imports into separate projects retained the tested version and review associations. The unreviewed revision stayed distinct from earlier assessments, and excluded content was marked unavailable. A separate registry case linked a table to its recorded task, execution and review. Offline re-execution of its retained script on a fixed input reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte. Limitations stated by the paper include that the controlled test used one session and one installation, that native input-edge rows were absent, and that initial task attribution still depends on the surrounding conversation.

digest_headlines.heading: Author affiliations
digest_headlines.headline: The author list spans many hospitals and companies, mainly in China, with affiliations also in the Netherlands, Israel and the United States.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sharing AI-assisted research needs its task, version and review relations to survive transfer, not only the output files.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier provenance and session-sharing systems cover parts of the problem; this work focuses on version and review attribution after exchange.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods and implementation
digest_headlines.headline: The method maps workbench records into typed objects and relations, then checks an exported package against an independently extracted source reference.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Relations, not just files, survived export in a controlled session, with all paired comparisons matching in both exchange conditions.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: A failed assessment, its correction and an unreviewed revision can all be true together, so exchange must keep each target separate.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The contract keeps recorded version and review relations across identifier mapping and explicit omissions, with evidence limited to the tested records.

digest_headlines.heading: Data and code availability
digest_headlines.headline: The software is released under Apache 2.0, and a de-identified validation release on Hugging Face contains the protocol, packages and audit scripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Declaration of AI assistance
digest_headlines.headline: Codex assisted with literature retrieval, source inspection, application operation and validation code, and the authors remain responsible for interpretation.

digest_headlines.heading: Supplementary Information
digest_headlines.headline: The supplementary figure lists case16 evidence associations and an offline re-execution that reproduced two saved tables byte for byte.

repos.title: Making Images Real Again: A Comprehensive Survey on Deep Image Composition
repos.paper_summary:
This paper surveys deep image composition, a task that combines foreground and background images to produce realistic composites. It decomposes the problem into sub-tasks: object placement, image blending, image harmonization, shadow generation, reflection generation, and generative composition. The authors categorize methods for each sub-task into traditional rule-based approaches and deep learning techniques, such as GANs and diffusion models. They also summarize available datasets and evaluation metrics, including FID, PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and user studies.

The paper releases `libcom`, a Python toolbox assembling over 10 functions for these tasks, and an online workbench. Experimental comparisons are provided on specific datasets like OPA (73,470 images) for object placement and iHarmony4 for harmonization. For instance, in object placement, discriminative approaches like FOPA outperform generative ones like PlaceNet. In painterly harmonization, diffusion-based methods like PHDiffusion outperform GAN-based baselines on challenging textures. Limitations include the high cost of collecting paired ground-truth data for harmonization and the difficulty of evaluating arbitrary compositions without dense annotations.

repos.title: Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation
repos.paper_summary: Hy-Nomas is an 8B-parameter video world model that generates interactive video from free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple turns. It is built on HunyuanVideo 1.5 and generates variable-length segments conditioned on the current input and cached history. Its main design choice is action-aware causal attention: structured captions describe persistent scene and subject context that stays visible to later segments, while timestamped action instructions are limited to their own time window. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts user requests and interaction history into structured conditions for each next segment. Training follows a multi-stage curriculum (causal generation, text interaction, camera control, training on model-generated histories), then diffusion distillation. Human evaluation is reported as favoring Hy-Nomas over existing world models, but the text provided does not include the scores. The paper notes that temporal causality does not establish physical causality, that robotics adaptation is shown only as an initial LoRA demonstration, and that retrieving past views does not update off-screen state, such as a clock that should keep running. Weights, code, and benchmarks are released.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hy-Nomas is an 8B interactive world model that follows free-form text and camera commands across multiple turns.

digest_headlines.heading: Data
digest_headlines.headline: Training videos are filtered, deduplicated, and annotated with camera trajectories and structured captions.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Action-aware causal attention limits each action to its own time window, and camera tokens condition each segment.

digest_headlines.heading: Training Infrastructure
digest_headlines.headline: Sequence parallelism, compute-balanced packing and masked attention kernels support training on sequences up to 360K tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Training
digest_headlines.headline: Training proceeds through causal, interaction and context curricula, then distillation from 100 to 4 steps per segment.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Inference
digest_headlines.headline: A vision-language Prompt Enhancer turns user requests into segment captions, and inference is optimized for a single device.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Human raters prefer Hy-Nomas over three interactive world models on most tasks, but Genie 3 leads on spatial memory.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Hy-Nomas is placed among video-based world models that add text and camera control to diffusion video generators.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Future Directions
digest_headlines.headline: Discussion names open challenges: response latency, action-grounded robotics, retrieval-based memory, and detailed caption quality.

digest_headlines.heading: Contributors
digest_headlines.headline: Contributors section lists core contributors, contributors, acknowledgments and leadership acknowledgments.

repos.title: Monocular Identity-Conditioned Facial Reflectance Reconstruction
repos.paper_summary: ID2Reflectance is a framework for monocular facial reflectance reconstruction that estimates diffuse albedo, specular albedo, roughness, and surface normal maps from a single in-the-wild image. The method learns a facial prior in image space rather than UV space to reduce dependency on limited light-stage data. It trains a VQGAN with multi-domain codebooks, aligning RGB and reflectance domains by jointly training on FFHQ and 135 captured subjects. An identity-conditioned swapper module, trained on VGGFace2HQ using AdaIN, injects identity features from the target image into the pre-trained decoder. At inference, the system synthesizes three-view reflectance images and stitches them into UV-space maps. On a test set of 20 subjects, ID2Reflectance achieves a PSNR of 28.47 dB for diffuse albedo, outperforming TRUST (21.63 dB) and ID2Albedo (23.72 dB). Identity similarity reaches 0.735 compared to 0.532 for ID2Albedo. The total inference time is 3.8 seconds per face on an A6000 GPU. The paper notes that reconstructed PBR maps may not be physically plausible due to the lack of ground-truth supervision.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Reflectance models trained on few light-stage captures generalize poorly, so the method learns the reflectance prior in image space from abundant RGB faces.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior facial reflectance methods depend on light-stage data and their data is unreleased, while face swapping methods target only the RGB domain.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Two-stage codebook training aligns reflectance with RGB, so identity swapping learned on RGB transfers to reflectance maps.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Trained on 115 captured subjects, the method gives identity-preserved reflectance on Digital Emily and in-the-wild faces in 3.8 seconds/face.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions and Discussions
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that limited captured data yields a reliable reflectance prior and notes the method could be misused.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the light stage rig, public datasets, codebook and swapper details, UV stitching, a fairness benchmark, and further qualitative results.

repos.title: OpenEBFM: Energy-based Foundation Models Are Scalable Architecture
repos.paper_summary:
It proposes Energy-Based Foundation Models (EBFMs), a language model that pairs an energy head with a token generator. At inference, a latent state starts from a standard Gaussian and takes K gradient-descent steps on an energy function with model weights fixed. The generative head then predicts tokens from the refined latent. Training computes steered latents at all positions in one forward pass using a redesigned attention mask, minimizing next-token negative log-likelihood.

Models with 12, 20 and 26 layers (up to 1.03B parameters) were pre-trained on Fineweb, ClimbMix and DCLM and compared with GPTs by validation bits per byte. On ClimbMix, the three EBFMs match GPT performance at 7B tokens after 4.5B, 3.5B and 5.1B training tokens. On DCLM, EBFM error falls faster than GPT error as parameters grow from 268M to 1.03B. The abstract claims EBFMs beat GPTs on most of 26 zero-shot tasks (19 QA tasks plus seven generation datasets), but the provided text lacks task-level results.

Limitations: training uses data parallelism because existing sharding frameworks lack the second-order gradients EBM training needs, so each model must fit on one GPU. Block-wise energy steering is left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing energy-based models are limited to single domains, so this paper proposes energy-based foundation models for general language modeling.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminary
digest_headlines.headline: Preliminaries define an energy head and a generative head that share one Transformer backbone.

digest_headlines.heading: Energy-based Foundation Models
digest_headlines.headline: Energy steering refines a latent state by gradient descent on the energy, and training runs this for all positions in parallel.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation Results
digest_headlines.headline: EBFMs match GPT validation error with fewer training tokens and outperform GPTs on most zero-shot question-answering tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Open-source Release
digest_headlines.headline: Training infrastructure, logs, and model weights are released publicly, with datasets linked in the released code.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations under Current Ecosystem
digest_headlines.headline: Scaling is limited because current parallelism tools lack second-order gradient support, and block-wise generation is future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Energy steering shows promising scaling across 19 downstream tasks, and the weights and infrastructure are fully released.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Directions
digest_headlines.headline: Suggested future work covers supervised fine-tuning, efficient inference and training algorithms, and distributed training infrastructure.

repos.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
repos.paper_summary: SpecPilot is an autonomous agentic loop that searches for lossless speculative decoding optimizations tailored to each deployment. A cost model ranks the largest gaps between the current system and an estimated speedup ceiling, parallel agents explore directions on separate GPUs, and a controller promotes only changes with a significant gain on unseen requests. Token forcing checks every output token against the stock engine, catching lossy changes that task accuracy misses. Validated mechanisms are stored in structured memory and reused across rounds and deployments. Discovered mechanisms include W12, a lossless 12-bit weight format averaging 12.01–12.02 bits per weight; best-first tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets; two-level verification using an 8-bit view of W12 as a low-precision pre-check; and three batching mechanisms. Across four target models, three drafters, two GPUs and five benchmarks, speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding rises from stock's 4.46× to 10.87× with one request, and from 1.94× to 3.93× with batching. On H100 with one request, the paper reports 1.84× faster than DDTree. The gains are reported without training or quality loss. Limitations: the loop depends on agent-driven search, and results are measured only on the listed models, drafters, GPUs and benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Stock parallel-drafter systems leave speedup unrealized, which motivates SpecPilot's per-deployment search.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Lossless speculative decoding accepts only tokens matching the exact target's argmax, so output tests cannot easily verify it.

digest_headlines.heading: SpecPilot
digest_headlines.headline: A cost model finds the largest gap to a ceiling, and a controller accepts changes only on confirmed gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Discovered Lossless Algorithms
digest_headlines.headline: SpecPilot discovered a lossless 12-bit weight format, best-first tree verification, two-level verification and batching mechanisms.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Sealed finals on unseen requests give single-request gains of 2.13× to 2.44× and batching gains of 1.85× to 3.11×.

repos.title: ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions
repos.paper_summary: ODE policy learns the dynamics of a robot action, modeling the policy as a neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) whose vector field is conditioned on the observation. Each action is integrated from the previous one at inference, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. In imitation learning, the field is trained by matching integrated action chunks to demonstrations, and a contractive perturbation of chunk start points pulls states back toward the demonstrations. An optional diversity head supports multi-modal behavior. On LIBERO, it reaches 79.2% success after one epoch, against at most 43.2% for baselines. As the action head of π0.5, it reaches 96.0% against 75.5% for flow matching. It generates a chunk 10.8 times faster than flow matching in simulation. It has the highest success rate on all 14 real-world tasks. As the actor of SuperMimic in RL, it ends training with a return of 0.885 against 0.845. Limitations: encoding the binary gripper command as a field state lowers LIBERO success after one epoch from 79.2% to 74.5%. Early model-free RL experiments showed little gain and sometimes a loss. Several analyses use a single seed.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Most robot policies map observations to discrete actions and leave continuity to be learned; ODE policy instead learns the action's dynamics.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior ODE robot policies fix the vector field's form, and efficiency methods keep direct-action actors, which ODE policy changes.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Direct-action policies output each action separately, while a neural ODE defines a field integrated over time.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method integrates a learned action field over each chunk, trains it on integrated paths, and adds a sampled diversity offset.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation compares ODE policy with 14 baselines on simulated and real tasks, with shared backbones, data, and training schedules.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulation Results
digest_headlines.headline: In simulation, ODE policy learns faster, needs fewer demonstrations, generates actions faster, and keeps multiple behavior modes.

digest_headlines.heading: Real-World Results
digest_headlines.headline: On four real robots, ODE policy has the highest success rate on each reported task and transfers dexterous skills across labs.

digest_headlines.heading: Ablation Studies
digest_headlines.headline: Ablations show that chunking is essential and that removing the contractive perturbation drops the one-epoch success rate from 79.8% to 58.4%.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Future Directions
digest_headlines.headline: Discussion argues continuity built into the policy improves efficiency across scales and suggests three preliminary extensions.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists benchmark and robot details, training settings, timing tables, and extra generalization, multi-modal, and ablation results.

repos.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
repos.paper_summary: The Switch Transformer replaces the standard feed-forward layer in Transformers with a sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) module that routes each token to a single expert, reducing communication overhead and improving training stability. By using top-1 routing instead of top-k, the model maintains constant computational cost per token while scaling parameter count. The paper introduces selective precision casting to stabilize bfloat16 training and an auxiliary load-balancing loss to ensure uniform expert usage. Experiments on the C4 corpus show that a 64-expert Switch-Base model achieves the same pre-training quality as T5-Base in one-seventh the time. Fine-tuning results indicate consistent improvements over T5-Base and T5-Large on GLUE, SuperGLUE, SQuAD, and summarization tasks. Distilling these sparse models into dense T5-Base architectures preserves approximately 30% of the quality gain while compressing model size by up to 99%. In multilingual settings across 101 languages, the method yields a mean 5x speedup over mT5-Base. A limitation is that distillation does not fully recover teacher performance, and the approach relies on specific hardware parallelism strategies for trillion-parameter scales.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse expert routing is proposed to add parameters without raising per-example compute, with gains across pre-training, fine-tuning and multilingual training.

digest_headlines.heading: Switch Transformer
digest_headlines.headline: Routing each token to one expert simplifies Mixture of Experts, with capacity limits and a balancing loss keeping training stable.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling Properties
digest_headlines.headline: Increasing experts at fixed FLOPS per token speeds up pre-training, with Switch-Base 64 reaching T5-Base quality in one-seventh the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Downstream Results
digest_headlines.headline: Switch models improve most T5 fine-tuning tasks, distill to dense models keeping 30% of gains, and beat mT5 on all 101 languages.

digest_headlines.heading: Designing Models with Data, Model, and Expert-Parallelism
digest_headlines.headline: Data, model and expert parallelism combine to train 395 billion and 1.6 trillion parameter Switch models, with Switch-XXL sometimes unstable.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work scales models through model parallelism and conditional computation, including mixture of experts and attention sparsity.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse models are argued to outperform dense models per step and on wall clock time, but distilled versions keep only about 30% of gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Remaining challenges include stabilizing the largest models, heterogeneous experts, expert layers beyond feed-forward layers, and other modalities.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Switch Transformers are presented as stable, sample-efficient language learners across pre-training, fine-tuning and multi-task training.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers attention Switch layers, token rerouting, router exploration, small-scale results, upstream-downstream correlation and pseudocode.

repos.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
repos.paper_summary:
Graph RAG is a method for answering global questions over large text corpora by using an LLM to build an entity knowledge graph and pre-generate hierarchical community summaries. The pipeline extracts entities and relationships from source text chunks, partitions the resulting graph into communities using the Leiden algorithm, and summarizes each community. At query time, it generates partial answers from community summaries in parallel and synthesizes them into a final response. This differs from standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which retrieves local text chunks and fails on corpus-wide sensemaking questions.

The authors evaluated Graph RAG against naïve RAG and a map-reduce baseline that summarizes raw source texts directly. They used two datasets of approximately 1 million tokens and 125 LLM-generated sensemaking questions per dataset. An LLM-as-a-judge assessed answers on comprehensiveness, diversity, empowerment, and directness. Global approaches outperformed naïve RAG, with comprehensiveness win rates between 72% and 83%. Intermediate-level community summaries provided better comprehensiveness and diversity than source-text summarization while using 26–33% fewer context tokens. Root-level summaries reduced token usage by over 97% compared to source-text processing. Limitations include evaluation on only two specific datasets and question types, with no validation of fabrication rates or end-user utility.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: RAG cannot answer corpus-wide sensemaking questions, so GraphRAG builds an entity graph with community summaries and outperforms vector RAG with GPT-4.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers graph-based retrieval, hierarchical summaries and benchmarks oriented toward explicit fact retrieval rather than global questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: GraphRAG extracts an entity graph, detects Leiden communities, summarizes them, and answers queries by map-reduce over summaries.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments compare six conditions on two corpora of about one million tokens, using generated global sensemaking questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: Global GraphRAG conditions beat vector RAG on comprehensiveness at 72-83% win rates on podcast transcripts.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluation covers only two corpora and lacks a fabrication-rate comparison, which the authors name as limitations.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Root-level community summaries give a data index that beats vector RAG and competes with other global methods at lower token cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists extraction prompts, self-reflection gleaning, community detection, context window tests, an example comparison, and system prompts.

repos.title: RAG-Anything: All-in-One RAG Framework
repos.paper_summary: RAG-Anything is a unified multimodal retrieval-augmented generation framework that builds a dual graph over documents: a cross-modal graph anchored on non-text units (figures, tables, equations) and a text-based graph, merged by entity-name alignment. Retrieval combines graph neighborhood expansion with dense embedding search over entities, relations, and chunks, and a VLM answers using text context plus the dereferenced visual content. On DocBench, it reaches 63.4% overall accuracy versus 61.0% for MMGraphRAG, 58.4% for LightRAG, and 51.2% for GPT-4o-mini. On MMLongBench, it reaches 42.8% versus 38.9% for LightRAG and 37.7% for MMGraphRAG. The gap grows with document length: on DocBench it is over 13 points for documents over 100 pages. Ablations on DocBench show 60.0% for chunk-only retrieval and 62.4% without the reranker, against 63.4% for the full system. All baselines use GPT-4o-mini, and accuracy is judged by GPT-4o-mini. The paper reports no variance across runs. Evaluation covers two benchmarks only.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing RAG systems handle only text, so multimodal documents are poorly served; the paper proposes RAG-Anything to fix this.

digest_headlines.heading: The RAG-Anything Framework
digest_headlines.headline: RAG-Anything decomposes documents into typed units, builds two linked graphs, and retrieves through both structure and embeddings.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On MMLongBench, RAG-Anything scores 42.8% overall versus 37.7% for MMGraphRAG, with gains growing on longer documents.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work groups graph-enhanced RAG and multimodal RAG, and argues that prior multimodal systems fragment by modality.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that dual-graph retrieval helps long documents and identifies text-centric bias and rigid spatial processing as failure modes.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, extra case studies, the three multimodal prompts, the accuracy prompt, and failure-case analyses.
